# Data investigations - Practice Test - Year 9

Attempt all questions and show your working. Suggested time: 30 to 35 minutes.

## Section A: Consolidating (Questions 1-4)

**Question 1**

State the most suitable method of collecting data for each investigation: a survey, an observation, an experiment or a secondary source (data already collected by someone else).

(a) Finding how many cars turn right at an intersection between 8 am and 9 am

(b) Finding the favourite holiday destination of students in your year level

(c) Finding whether a paper aeroplane flies further with or without folded wing tips

(d) Finding the population of each Australian capital city over the last $50$ years

**Question 2**

A council wants to know whether the people living in a town support building a new skate park. There are $4500$ households in the town. The council sends a survey to $300$ households chosen at random.

(a) What is the population in this investigation?

(b) What is the sample, and what is the sample size?

(c) Give one reason the council might use a sample rather than survey every household.

**Question 3**

For each investigation, state whether a census (collecting data from the whole population) or a sample would be more suitable. Give a reason.

(a) A teacher wants the test results of every student in her class of $26$.

(b) A company wants to know how long its light globes last before failing, which means testing them until they stop working.

(c) A TV network wants to know which shows Australians watch most.

**Question 4**

Seven students recorded the number of text messages they sent before school one morning:

$8, \ 5, \ 13, \ 2, \ 6, \ 5, \ 10$

Find the mean, median, mode and range.

## Section B: Standard (Questions 5-16)

**Question 5**

Each of these survey questions has a problem. For each one, explain the problem and rewrite the question so it is fair.

(a) "Most people think our school uniform is ugly. Do you agree?"

(b) "How much do you spend on lunch each week? Tick one: \$0 to \$10, \$10 to \$20, \$20 or more."

(c) "Do you exercise a lot?"

**Question 6**

A school has $600$ students. A stratified random sample of $40$ students is chosen, so that each year level is represented in proportion to its size.

| Year level | 7 | 8 | 9 | 10 | 11 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Number of students | 150 | 120 | 135 | 105 | 90 |
| Number in sample | | | | | |

(a) Complete the table.

(b) Why is this sample better than surveying $40$ students from Year 9 only, if the school wants to know the views of all its students?

**Question 7**

Explain why each sample is likely to be biased (not representative of the population).

(a) To find out how people in a city travel to work, a researcher surveys people waiting on a train platform at 8 am.

(b) To find out whether Australians think more money should be spent on sport, a sports website runs an online poll.

(c) To find out whether students want the canteen to open earlier, Ethan asks the first $30$ students in the canteen line at 8:30 am.

**Question 8**

Ruby wants to investigate the question: "Do students who live further from school spend more time travelling to school?"

(a) Name the two variables Ruby needs to collect data on, and state the type of data for each.

(b) Describe a good way for Ruby to collect the data.

(c) What type of display should Ruby use to show the data? Explain.

(d) Give one possible source of error or bias in Ruby's investigation.

**Question 9**

The heights, in centimetres, of $12$ seedlings grown in an experiment were:

$13, \ 6, \ 21, \ 9, \ 4, \ 16, \ 12, \ 25, \ 7, \ 18, \ 10, \ 15$

(a) Find the median.

(b) Find the lower and upper quartiles. (Use the lower six and the upper six values.)

(c) Find the interquartile range and the range.

**Question 10**

A sample of $25$ households was asked how many people live in their home.

| Number of people | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Number of households | 3 | 8 | 5 | 6 | 3 |

(a) Find the mean number of people per household.

(b) Find the median.

(c) Find the mode.

**Question 11**

A class investigated whether Year 9 students complete a puzzle faster than Year 7 students. They timed a random sample of $20$ students from each year level. The results (in minutes) are summarised below.

| | Mean | Median | Range | Interquartile range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Year 7 | 4.2 | 4.0 | 3.5 | 1.5 |
| Year 9 | 3.1 | 3.0 | 2.5 | 1.0 |

(a) Which group was faster on average? Use a statistic to support your answer.

(b) Which group's times were more consistent? Use a statistic to support your answer.

(c) Write a one-sentence conclusion that answers the class's question.

**Question 12**

A random sample of $50$ of the $250$ Year 9 students at a school was surveyed. Of these, $18$ said they play club sport.

(a) What percentage of the sample play club sport?

(b) Estimate the number of Year 9 students at the school who play club sport.

(c) Another random sample of $50$ Year 9 students is taken. Will exactly $18$ of them play club sport? Explain.

**Question 13**

In a survey, $60$ Year 10 students and $60$ Year 12 students were asked whether they have a part-time job. Some values are missing from the table.

| | Job | No job | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Year 10 | 12 | | 60 |
| Year 12 | | 33 | 60 |
| Total | | | 120 |

(a) Complete the table.

(b) What percentage of Year 10 students and what percentage of Year 12 students have a part-time job?

(c) Write a conclusion about part-time jobs that the data supports.

**Question 14**

In a reaction time experiment, Kai recorded these times, in seconds, for six attempts:

$0.32, \ 0.28, \ 0.35, \ 0.30, \ 0.25, \ 3.00$

On the last attempt, Kai forgot to stop the timer straight away.

(a) Find the mean of all six times.

(b) Find the mean of the first five times.

(c) Should Kai include the last time in his results? Explain.

**Question 15**

Answer these questions about planning a statistical investigation.

(a) Explain the difference between primary data and secondary data.

(b) Give one advantage of using primary data and one advantage of using secondary data.

(c) Explain why it is important for a survey sample to be chosen at random.

**Question 16**

Two students estimated the percentage of students at their school who are left-handed.

- Tom asked $10$ of his friends and found that $3$ were left-handed.
- Priya chose $100$ students at random from the school roll and found that $11$ were left-handed.

(a) Write each student's result as a percentage.

(b) Whose estimate is likely to be more reliable? Give two reasons.

(c) The school has $900$ students. Use Priya's result to estimate the number of left-handed students at the school.

## Section C: Advanced (Questions 17-20)

**Question 17**

A class investigated whether listening to music affects memory. Ten students tried to remember a list of $20$ words while music played (Group M), and ten different students tried with no music (Group S). The numbers of words remembered were:

Group M: $9, \ 12, \ 8, \ 11, \ 10, \ 7, \ 13, \ 10, \ 9, \ 11$

Group S: $12, \ 14, \ 11, \ 15, \ 13, \ 12, \ 16, \ 10, \ 14, \ 13$

(a) Find the mean, median and range for each group.

(b) Write a conclusion for the investigation, using your statistics.

(c) Suggest one way to improve the investigation so the conclusion is more reliable.

**Question 18**

A sports club has $240$ members: $96$ juniors, $120$ seniors and $24$ veterans. The committee chooses a stratified random sample of $30$ members to ask whether they want a new club uniform.

(a) How many juniors, seniors and veterans should be in the sample?

(b) In the sample, $9$ juniors, $6$ seniors and $2$ veterans said they want a new uniform. Use these results to estimate the number of members in each group who want a new uniform.

(c) Estimate the total number of club members who want a new uniform. Does a majority of the club want one?

**Question 19**

Liam recorded the number of minutes he spent reading each day for $6$ days:

$25, \ 40, \ 30, \ 35, \ 20, \ 30$

(a) Find the mean for these $6$ days.

(b) How many minutes must Liam read on day $7$ for the mean of all $7$ days to be $32$ minutes?

(c) Find the median of the $7$ days if he reads that amount on day $7$.

**Question 20**

A newspaper headline says: "Survey shows $85\%$ of Australians love public transport!"

The survey was done by asking $200$ people waiting at city train stations: "Don't you think public transport is great?" Of these, $170$ answered yes.

(a) Check that $85\%$ is correct for the people surveyed.

(b) Describe three problems with how this investigation was carried out or reported.

(c) Describe a better way to collect data to answer the question "What percentage of Australians like public transport?"

# Data investigations - Answer Key

**Question 1**

Answer: (a) Observation (b) Survey (c) Experiment (d) Secondary source

**Question 2**

Answer: (a) All $4500$ households in the town (b) The $300$ randomly chosen households; sample size $300$ (c) A sample is cheaper and quicker (accept any sensible reason, such as less time or cost)

**Question 3**

Answer: (a) Census: the class is small and every result is needed. (b) Sample: testing destroys the globes, so testing them all would leave none to sell. (c) Sample: the population is far too large to ask everyone.

**Question 4**

Answer: Mean $7$ ($\frac{49}{7}$), median $6$, mode $5$, range $11$

**Question 5**

Answer: (a) Leading question that pushes people to agree; e.g. "What is your opinion of our school uniform?" with a rating scale (b) The categories overlap (\$10 and \$20 each fit two boxes); e.g. "\$0 to \$9.99, \$10 to \$19.99, \$20 or more" (c) "A lot" is vague and means different things to different people; e.g. "How many hours do you exercise in a typical week?" (accept any clear, specific question)

**Question 6**

Answer: (a) Year 7: $10$, Year 8: $8$, Year 9: $9$, Year 10: $7$, Year 11: $6$ (each is $\frac{40}{600}$ of the year level) (b) Every year level is represented in proportion to its size, so the sample is more likely to reflect the views of the whole school.

**Question 7**

Answer: (a) Only people who travel by train are asked, so drivers, cyclists and others are left out. (b) Only people who visit a sports website and choose to vote take part, and they are likely to support sport. (c) Only students who are already at school early and buying from the canteen are asked; they are more likely to want an earlier opening.

**Question 8**

Answer: (a) Distance from school (numerical, continuous) and travel time (numerical, continuous; accept discrete if recorded in whole minutes) (b) e.g. survey a random sample of students from all year levels asking for their distance and travel time (c) A scatter plot, because it shows the relationship between two numerical variables (d) e.g. students may guess or misremember distances or times, or the sample may not be random

**Question 9**

Answer: (a) $12.5 \text{ cm}$ (b) $Q_1 = 8 \text{ cm}$, $Q_3 = 17 \text{ cm}$ (c) IQR $= 9 \text{ cm}$, range $= 21 \text{ cm}$

**Question 10**

Answer: (a) $2.92$ ($\frac{73}{25}$) (b) $3$ (the 13th value) (c) $2$

**Question 11**

Answer: (a) Year 9: its mean ($3.1$ minutes) and median ($3.0$ minutes) are both lower. (b) Year 9: its range ($2.5$) and IQR ($1.0$) are both smaller. (c) e.g. Year 9 students in the sample completed the puzzle faster, and with more consistent times, than Year 7 students.

**Question 12**

Answer: (a) $36\%$ (b) $90$ students ($36\%$ of $250$) (c) Probably not. Different random samples give different results (sampling variation), although the result should be close.

**Question 13**

Answer: (a) Year 10 no job $48$; Year 12 job $27$; totals: Job $39$, No job $81$ (b) Year 10: $20\%$; Year 12: $45\%$ (c) e.g. A greater percentage of Year 12 students than Year 10 students in the survey have a part-time job.

**Question 14**

Answer: (a) $0.75 \text{ s}$ ($\frac{4.5}{6}$) (b) $0.30 \text{ s}$ ($\frac{1.5}{5}$) (c) No. The $3.00$ s time is an outlier caused by a recording error, so it does not measure Kai's reaction time and would distort the mean.

**Question 15**

Answer: (a) Primary data is collected by the investigator; secondary data has already been collected by someone else. (b) e.g. Primary: it is collected for exactly the question being asked. Secondary: it is quick and cheap to get, and may cover a large population. (c) So that every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen, which avoids bias and makes the sample more likely to be representative.

**Question 16**

Answer: (a) Tom $30\%$, Priya $11\%$ (b) Priya's: her sample is larger ($100$ compared with $10$), and it is chosen at random, while Tom's friends may not be representative. (c) $99$ students ($11\%$ of $900$)

**Question 17**

Answer: (a) Group M: mean $10$, median $10$, range $6$. Group S: mean $13$, median $13$, range $6$ (b) e.g. Students remembered more words with no music (mean and median both $3$ words higher), and both groups were equally spread, so music seemed to reduce memory in this investigation. (c) e.g. use larger groups, allocate students to groups at random, or have each student try both conditions

**Question 18**

Answer: (a) Juniors $12$, seniors $15$, veterans $3$ (b) Juniors $72$ ($\frac{9}{12} \times 96$), seniors $48$ ($\frac{6}{15} \times 120$), veterans $16$ ($\frac{2}{3} \times 24$) (c) $136$ members; yes, $136$ is more than half of $240$

**Question 19**

Answer: (a) $30$ minutes ($\frac{180}{6}$) (b) $44$ minutes ($32 \times 7 = 224$, $224 - 180 = 44$) (c) $30$ minutes

**Question 20**

Answer: (a) $\frac{170}{200} \times 100 = 85\%$, correct (b) Any three of: the sample only includes people at city train stations, who already use public transport; the question is leading; the sample does not represent all Australians (no country areas, non-users); the headline says "love" when people were only asked whether it is "great". (c) e.g. ask a large random sample of Australians from different cities and country areas a neutral question such as "How do you rate public transport?" with a rating scale
